newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ RETAIL DATA SEEN SHOWING WEAK ECONOMIC BOUNCE.
newsitem.headline: NZ RETAIL DATA SEEN SHOWING WEAK ECONOMIC BOUNCE.

text.p: Retail trade data this week is expected to back the view that the New Zealand economy rebounded slightly in the June quarter, but economists are loath to read too much into the numbers.
On average, economists polled by Reuters forecast seasonally adjusted retail sales will rise 1.21 percent in the June quarter, following a March quarter fall of one percent.
The economists saw actual sales in the quarter falling 0.17 percent against the June 1996 quarter, following a two percent fall in the March quarter from the March 1996 quarter.
Bankers Trust New Zealand (BTNZ) said the data release was likely to conform with the central bank's view of a June quarter rebound in economic activity.

"I think what that reflects is just the trading day effect of the shift in the timing of Easter. That tended to depress the March quarter significantly, and as that unwinds, the June quarter gets pushed up," BTNZ chief economist David Plank told Reuters Financial Television.
He noted that Statistics New Zealand did not make any adjustment for shifts in the timing of public holidays.

"That can have a big impact on the data and we're seeing that, so I don't think you can read too much into the quarterly numbers. What it does show, though, is that for the first six months of the year the economy was pretty flat. It wasn't negative -- I think growth over the six months will be positive, but the economy basically is at the bottom," Plank told RFTV.

UBS Australia economist Stephen Roberts said that like the June quarter household labour force data released last week, the retail trade numbers would be consistent with a weak bounce in economic activity in the June quarter.

"Also, like the household labour force data, the fine detail of the retail trade report is more likely to raise questions about the sustainability of the bounce, rather than encourage expectations that economic growth is through the trough and starting to accelerate," Roberts said.
He said UBS Australia still saw weak annual economic growth below two percent in the second half of 1997, well below potential growth around 2.75 percent.
